title: Corrosion behaviour of mild steel in diverse environments: a comparative study of hot-rolled and cold-rolled specimens
abstract: Abstract Materials undergo degradation and structural failure due to corrosion, leading to substantial economic losses in industrial applications. This study investigates the corrosion behavior and mechanical degradation of hot-rolled and cold-rolled mild steel in six different environments (air, tap water, seawater, NaCl, HCl, and H₂SO₄) over a period of 30 days. The analysis included weight loss, corrosion rate, thickness reduction, and mechanical strength evaluations at multiple intervals. Results revealed that cold-rolled specimens suffered up to a 55% loss in elongation and a 40% decline in tensile strength, particularly in acidic conditions. The superior performance of hot-rolled steel highlights the influence of manufacturing methods on corrosion resistance. Among all tested environments, sulfuric acid proved to be the most aggressive, with cold-rolled steel specimens exhibiting 10.212 mm and 5.649 mm of corrosion compared to 9.488 mm and 5.577 mm for hot-rolled steel specimens during the 30-day exposure period. Sulfuric acid exposure caused a maximum thickness reduction of 38.12%, along with a 40% loss in tensile strength and a 55% reduction in elongation at break for cold-rolled steel. Under the same exposure conditions, the compressive strength of hot-rolled specimens decreased by 25%. This comparative study offers valuable insights for designing durable steel structures and developing advanced corrosion mitigation strategies.
journal: Journal of King Saud University – Engineering Sciences

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Corrosion is an unavoidable and widespread problem that poses significant challenges to industries worldwide by degrading materials, causing structural failures, and leading to major financial losses (Gardner et al.  8 ). The global economy suffers trillions of dollars in annual losses due to corrosion damage, with sectors such as construction, transportation, energy production, and manufacturing bearing a substantial share of this impact (Gong et al.  10 ). Mild steel is widely used in these industries due to its availability, cost-effectiveness, and favorable engineering properties (Seshweni et al.  32 ). However, its susceptibility to various corrosive agents remains a critical concern for manufacturers. Evaluating the corrosion behavior of mild steel under diverse conditions is therefore essential for selecting optimal materials, designing durable structures, and implementing effective corrosion control strategies (Padilha et al.  21 ).

The deterioration of materials through electrochemical processes affects metals when they come into contact with their surrounding environment (Pour-Ali et al.  27 ). Material composition, environmental characteristics, and corrosive agents such as moisture, oxygen, salts, and acids determine the rate and extent of corrosion (Nandi et al.  17 ). Mild steel, which contains iron along with trace amounts of carbon and alloying elements, exhibits high sensitivity to corrosion because iron naturally reacts with its environment (Yeğen and Usta  36 ). When exposed to corrosive conditions, mild steel develops rust (iron oxide) through oxidation, leading to material degradation and structural breakdown (Ibrahim et al.  11 ; Wang et al.  35 ).Park et al. (Nie et al.  19 ) studied the corrosion behaviour of Cu- and Sb-alloyed cold-rolled and hot-rolled steels in FGD environments. Petcherdchoo (Petcherdchoo  26 ) highlighted the importance of considering both cost and environmental impacts when maintaining deteriorating reinforced concrete bridges. The study showed that combining silane treatment (SL) with minor repairs and rebuilds can improve structural condition and safety while reducing cumulative maintenance costs over 50 years. The findings suggest that SL is more cost-effective and environmentally friendly compared to cathodic protection (CP), which, while highly effective, results in much higher expenses and resource consumption. Integrating such strategies supports sustainable infrastructure management by balancing performance improvements with long-term economic and ecological benefits.Sherief (Al Kiey et al.  1 ) demonstrated the exceptional effectiveness of the green inhibitor subphthalocyanine chloride (SubPc) for protecting mild steel in acidic environments, achieving up to 97.6% efficiency at 150 ppm in 1 M HCl. Electrochemical analyses revealed that SubPc significantly reduces corrosion current density and hydrogen evolution by forming a protective barrier on the steel surface, thus blocking H⁺ ions and preventing metal dissolution. The use of such environmentally benign, cost-effective inhibitors aligns with sustainable industrial practices, offering a promising alternative to traditional toxic inhibitors. Further research is encouraged to optimize dosage and assess long-term performance in diverse acidic conditions. Using weight loss, EIS, SEM, XRD, and EDS, the study found that alloyed steels exhibited enhanced corrosion resistance, with hot-rolled specimens performing slightly better due to protective oxide layer formation. Nie et al. (Park et al.  23 ) evaluated the mechanical properties of steels used in CFS structures at temperatures up to 800 °C. They observed significant reductions in strength and ductility with increasing temperature, driven by microstructural changes, and emphasized the importance of accounting for fire-induced degradation in structural design. Biao Nie et al. (Nie et al.  18 ) investigated the effect of corrosion on CFS beam-columns under compression and bending. Their results showed notable reductions in strength, stiffness, and altered failure modes due to corrosion, reinforcing the need to account for corrosion in both design and maintenance.The rate at which mild steel corrodes depends strongly on environmental exposure (Yeğen and Usta  36 ). Atmospheric conditions promote rapid rust formation through the presence of moisture and oxygen, whereas aqueous conditions accelerate corrosion in the presence of salts and acids (Ibrahim et al.  11 ). The most aggressive conditions for mild steel occur in industrial environments where operations involve hydrochloric acid (HCl) and sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) (Wang et al.  35 ). These acids are widely used in chemical processing, metal cleaning operations, and various industrial applications, but their damaging effects on mild steel must be carefully considered (Panigrahi et al.  22 ).The price difference between cold-rolled (CR) and hot-rolled (HR) steel is also a key factor in material selection for engineering and building construction in India. As a rule, hot-rolled steel is more economical. In 2024, the price of hot-rolled steel in India ranged from ₹55,000 to ₹60,000 per metric ton. It is commonly used in structural parts, large machinery, and applications where surface finish and tight dimensional tolerance are not critical. Cold-rolled steel, however, undergoes additional processing (cold reduction, annealing, and temper rolling), resulting in improved surface finish, tighter tolerances, and enhanced strength. These improvements increase production costs, making cold-rolled steel 20–30% more expensive, at ₹70,000–₹80,000 per metric ton. While cold-rolled steel offers better mechanical performance and surface appearance, it is generally reserved for applications requiring precise forming, such as automobile body panels, home appliances, and precision parts. Conversely, hot-rolled steel retains a cost advantage in large-scale structural and load-bearing components, where economy and bulk strength are priorities. The method of manufacturing mild steel, combined with external influences, significantly affects its corrosion resistance (Clover et al.  5 ). Both hot-rolling and cold-rolling produce mild steel, but with distinct microstructural and mechanical characteristics (Seghier et al.  31 ). Hot-rolled steel develops a microstructure with larger grains, offering lower strength and hardness but excellent ductility (Jin et al.  12 ). Cold-rolled steel, processed at or near room temperature, achieves higher strength and hardness with reduced ductility due to its refined microstructure (Frommeyer et al.  7 ). In engineering and construction, hot-rolled steel is typically used for large structural members such as I-beams, channels, railroad tracks, and heavy-duty frames in bridges, buildings, and machines—applications where lower dimensional accuracy and rougher surfaces are acceptable. Cold-rolled steel, with its superior surface quality and precision, is preferred for applications where appearance and close tolerances matter, such as automobile body panels, household appliances, precision tubes, and metal furniture. The choice between the two depends on mechanical requirements, fabrication needs, and intended use. Material microstructure, linked to mechanical properties, influences corrosion behaviour because defects, residual stresses, and surface roughness serve as initiation sites for localized corrosion (Zeuner et al.  37 ). Research on mild steel corrosion behaviour in various environments is extensive because of its widespread use. Common corrosion control measures include protective coatings, cathodic protection, and corrosion inhibitors. However, optimizing material selection for specific environments is critical, as existing methods often add complexity and cost (Paul et al.  24 ; Ralston and Birbilis  28 ). Understanding corrosion mechanisms and the factors influencing corrosion rates is essential for proper evaluation. While there is considerable research on mild steel corrosion, few studies provide a comprehensive comparison of hot-rolled and cold-rolled mild steel across multiple environmental conditions (Seghier et al.  30 ). Most prior work focuses on individual environments or corrosion mechanisms, overlooking the influence of manufacturing methods on overall corrosion resistance (Eskandari et al.  6 ; Paul et al.  25 ). Moreover, the combined effects of corrosion and mechanical deterioration—particularly tensile and compressive strength changes—remain underexplored in structural engineering contexts (Balakrishnan et al.  2 ).The present research addresses these gaps by examining the corrosion patterns of hot-rolled and cold-rolled mild steel in six environments: air, three water types, sodium chloride solution, hydrochloric acid, and sulfuric acid. The study evaluates weight loss, corrosion rate, thickness variation, and mechanical property changes over 30 days, comparing the behaviour of hot-rolled and cold-rolled specimens to assess the influence of manufacturing processes on corrosion resistance.

The research environments were selected for their practical relevance to real-life conditions. Mild steel was tested in three primary settings: air, representing typical atmospheric exposure; tap water, simulating water distribution systems; and seawater, replicating marine and aquatic structures. Sodium chloride was included as an additive to replicate the corrosive effects of coastal areas and de-icing salts, both of which accelerate material deterioration. Severe industrial conditions were represented using hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid, both of which pose significant corrosion threats to mild steel. The study evaluates how mild steel behaves under these environments by examining its corrosion characteristics and the resulting changes in mechanical properties, including tensile strength, compressive strength, and elongation. Since the structural stability of mild steel components depends heavily on these properties, corrosion-related deterioration can compromise both safety and functional performance. The research tracks changes in these mechanical properties over time to quantify corrosion-induced degradation and identify the most aggressive environments. The findings are expected to have a substantial impact on industrial material selection and corrosion mitigation strategies. By comparing the corrosion behaviour of hot-rolled and cold-rolled mild steel, the study will enable engineers and designers to make informed choices for specific applications. Data on mechanical degradation will also enhance predictive models for estimating the service life of mild steel components in corrosive environments. Ultimately, the results will support the design of durable, cost-effective structures that minimize corrosion-related expenses.

This research presents an extensive investigation into mild steel corrosion, examining the influence of manufacturing processes alongside corrosion and mechanical wear phenomena. It addresses major gaps in current literature, aiming to provide practical insights for optimizing material selection and developing effective corrosion management techniques. The outcomes will benefit a wide range of industries by advancing both corrosion science and engineering practice.

sections.heading: Test materials
paragraphs:
The researchers selected hot-rolled mild steel and cold-rolled mild steel to analyse their corrosion behaviour across different environments. The distinct manufacturing processes of these steel types result in notable differences in microstructure, mechanical properties, and residual stress profiles, which in turn influence their corrosion performance. Table  1  presents the basic mechanical properties and chemical compositions of the tested steels, providing clarity on their material characteristics and aiding in the interpretation of their behaviour under various corrosion conditions. The study involved fabricating two types of experimental test specimens: cylindrical tubes and standard coupon shapes. The tube specimens measured 150 mm in length, 26 mm in outer diameter, and 2 mm in wall thickness. This configuration was chosen to replicate thin-walled structural components, which are more susceptible to both uniform and localized corrosion. Standard specimens were prepared according to relevant testing standards, as shown in Fig.  1 . A total of 72 specimens (36 coupons and 36 tube specimens) made from both hot-rolled and cold-rolled steel were exposed to six different environments, with three duplicates in each category. These specimens were used to measure mass loss, surface degradation, and changes in mechanical properties after the exposure period. Coupons were fabricated to precise dimensions, as any deviation could affect the measured surface area and the calculated corrosion rate. Before testing, all specimens underwent visual examination and a cleaning process to remove surface contaminants that could distort results. The preparation procedure involved cleaning with acetone, rinsing with distilled water, and air drying, ensuring all samples started from equivalent conditions. The comparison between hot-rolled and cold-rolled steel allowed the researchers to assess the influence of different rolling temperatures and mechanical processing on corrosion behaviour. Hot-rolled steel generally exhibits a rougher surface texture with larger crystal structures, while cold-rolled steel has a smoother surface with finer microstructures. Microstructural analysis confirmed these differences: optical microscopy revealed that cold-rolled specimens possess a finer, more homogeneous grain structure with higher dislocation densities due to plastic deformation during rolling, whereas hot-rolled specimens exhibit coarser, equiaxed grains with lower dislocation density. This explains the higher susceptibility of cold-rolled specimens to acid attack and the superior resistance of hot-rolled specimens to localized corrosion.

sections.heading: Experimental equipment
paragraphs: The experimental analysis of mild steel corrosion and mechanical properties employed several precise measurement devices throughout its duration. A digital balance with a precision of ± 0.001 g was used for mass measurements. Calculating the corrosion rate required accurate mass readings at both the beginning and end of the test, which were then used to determine weight loss per unit surface area over the exposure period(Nocito and Dibenedetto  20 ; Lasek and Mazancová  15 ). Prior to weighing, the samples were carefully dried and cleaned to prevent moisture interference or ongoing corrosion. Dimensional data, particularly sample thickness, was measured using a digital Vernier caliper (Fig.  3 (b)) with a precision of ± 0.01 mm. This proved essential for analyzing material loss and distinguishing between uniform and pitting corrosion. The test medium required constant monitoring with a calibrated pH meter (Fig.  3 (a)) to prevent unintended chemical changes(Bertolini et al.  3 ; Kus et al.  14 ). The measurement of pH values during tests proved essential because significant changes occurred in acidic and alkaline conditions which modified corrosion speed. Regular checks verified that the corrosion environment conditions stayed stable until deviations became visible for further evaluation within the analysis. A tensile and compression testing machine of AMIL, modelAIM-653–1 of 1000 KN following the ASTM E8 standards determines mechanical characteristics before corrosion exposure along with a subsequent evaluation after corrosion exposure. A tensile testing machine measured ultimate tensile strength changes and yield strength and elongation but a compression apparatus tested the load resistance of the tube specimens. Testing machines received calibration procedures in advance to confirm accurate and repeatable data results. The evaluation process incorporated both a magnifying lamp and a stereomicroscope as equipment for examining the surface(Geetha Devi et al.  9 ; Kannan et al.  13 ; Sirohi et al.  33 ). Researchers used this tool to examine the tube specimens under corrosive conditions and identify the development of surface defects and cracks as well as pitting formation. The combination of these instruments provided a comprehensive dataset to analyze not only mass and dimensional losses but also the mechanical degradation caused by corrosion(Venkatesan et al.  34 ; Chung et al.  4 ; Zheng et al.  38 ). Proper handling, calibration, and operation of the equipment were rigorously maintained to ensure experimental reliability and validity. Fig. 3 Instruments used for corrosion study

sections.heading: Condition of the test medium
paragraphs: The study examined the behaviour of mild steel in six different environments representing both natural settings and industrial situations. These included ambient air, running water, and seawater, as well as 1 M solutions of NaCl, HCl, and H₂SO₄. All testing environments underwent careful preparation and continuous maintenance throughout the experimental period to ensure reproducibility and consistency (Lins et al.  16 ; Reddy et al.  29 ). Exposure in ambient air allowed the investigation of oxidation processes occurring under dry atmospheric conditions. Freshwater exposure via running water replicated typical environmental corrosion patterns, while synthetic seawater simulated chloride concentrations characteristic of aggressive marine conditions. The three chemical solutions provided controlled, accelerated corrosion conditions. For the 1 M NaCl solution, 58.44 g of sodium chloride was dissolved in 1000 mL of distilled water, creating saltwater conditions similar to those found in de-icing systems and coastal infrastructure. Preparation of the 1 M HCl solution required the precise addition of 8.3 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid to 1000 mL of distilled water. Hydrochloric acid promotes both uniform and localized corrosion, making it suitable for severe acidic corrosion testing. The 1 M H₂SO₄ solution was prepared by slowly diluting 27.42 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid into 1000 mL of distilled water. The presence of sulfuric acid in industrial emissions and acid rain makes it an important medium for evaluating material resistance in such conditions.

Although all acidic and saline media were standardised at 1 M concentration, molarity alone does not fully define corrosive strength. Factors such as pH, ion mobility, and redox potential significantly influence corrosion behaviour. HCl and H₂SO₄, with their very low pH values, are more aggressive than neutral NaCl. Hydrochloric acid typically promotes uniform corrosion and pitting, while sulfuric acid may cause localized attack or passivation depending on the surface condition of the material. In contrast, NaCl primarily causes pitting without acid-induced dissolution. These distinctions were considered when interpreting results, and future work may include electrochemical techniques for more detailed corrosion analysis.

All solutions were prepared using distilled water to eliminate unknown ions that could alter corrosion rates. A calibrated pH meter ensured accurate and regular pH measurements, particularly in acidic media where small changes can strongly influence corrosion behaviour. Solutions were stored in corrosion-resistant polyethylene containers to prevent contamination. During immersion tests, samples were fully submerged to ensure uniform exposure across all surfaces. The solutions were regularly checked and replenished to maintain their molarity and volume, compensating for evaporation or contamination. This controlled preparation and maintenance ensured that observed material degradation could be confidently attributed to the intended environmental conditions, thereby improving the reliability and credibility of the corrosion performance data.

sections.heading: Mass loss analysis of coupon specimens under corrosive environments
paragraphs:
The mass loss data for cold-rolled and hot-rolled mild steel coupons under various environmental exposures (Table  2 ) provide valuable insights into the corrosion mechanisms involved. All reported values represent the average of three replicates. Based on observed variability, the standard deviation typically ranged from ± 0.02 g to ± 0.08 g across specimens, reflecting only minor inconsistencies in corrosion behaviour and measurement precision. The severity of corrosion in each medium is directly linked to its chemical nature and the microstructural features of the steel specimens. In neutral environments such as air and tap water, both steels exhibited negligible mass loss (< 1%), indicating minimal electrochemical activity. The absence of aggressive ions and relatively high pH levels likely suppressed anodic dissolution, maintaining the passive oxide layer on the steel surface. The slightly higher corrosion in air compared to tap water may be due to atmospheric humidity and the possibility of localised condensation, which can intermittently initiate mild surface oxidation. In saline environments such as seawater and NaCl solution, moderate corrosion was observed. Chloride ions, known for their ability to disrupt passive oxide films, promoted pitting corrosion—particularly in cold-rolled specimens. The finer grain structure and higher dislocation density of cold-rolled steel provide more active sites for localised attack, explaining the greater weight loss in cold-rolled coupons (1.163% in seawater) compared to hot-rolled ones (0.780%). Nevertheless, the overall corrosion rate remained lower than in acidic environments due to the buffering capacity and moderate pH of these saline media. In highly acidic environments—particularly HCl and H₂SO₄—extensive corrosion occurred due to the high concentration of hydrogen ions, which accelerate anodic dissolution of iron. The hydrogen evolution reaction dominated the cathodic process in these media, leading to rapid metal thinning and loss of integrity. Cold-rolled steel showed more severe degradation (30.233% in H₂SO₄ and 13.76% in HCl) than hot-rolled steel (24.025% and 9.984%, respectively). This higher susceptibility is primarily due to its finer microstructure and residual stresses from strain hardening, which increase electrochemical activity. These structural characteristics enhance anodic reaction kinetics and raise surface energy, making cold-rolled steel more vulnerable in low-pH conditions. Differences in corrosion resistance between the two steel types can also be attributed to their manufacturing processes. Hot-rolled steel, with its coarser grain size and lower dislocation density, is less reactive and offers greater resistance in aggressive environments. Its microstructural stability slows penetration of corrosive agents and delays passive film breakdown, resulting in lower weight loss overall.

sections.heading: Influence of environmental exposure on ductility and elongation behaviour
paragraphs:
The evaluation of elongation at break for cold-rolled and hot-rolled mild steel coupons under different corrosion environments (Table  3 ) reveals how ductility degrades due to electrochemical attack and microstructural damage. These changes are not merely numerical but signify fundamental shifts in the material’s failure behaviour—from ductile to brittle—depending on the environment’s aggressiveness. In the nominal condition, the cold-rolled specimen exhibited a higher elongation at break (38.107 mm) compared to hot-rolled steel (23.937 mm), owing to its finer grain structure and strain-hardened matrix, both of which enhance ductility in uncorroded conditions. Air exposure caused negligible degradation, with cold-rolled elongation reducing by only 8.8%, while hot-rolled showed a slight increase (0.96%), possibly due to relaxation of residual stresses or superficial oxidation that did not penetrate deeply. This confirms the minimal corrosive effect of atmospheric conditions and the preservation of ductile fracture modes. In tap water, the onset of electrochemical activity caused a measurable drop in ductility. Local destabilisation of the passive oxide film reduced elongation by 15.3% in cold-rolled steel and 14.1% in hot-rolled steel. While not severely aggressive, this indicates incipient corrosion weakening the matrix. Seawater and NaCl solutions, rich in chloride ions, had a more substantial impact, especially on hot-rolled steel. Chloride ions undermine passive films and initiate pitting corrosion, leading to stress concentration zones that accelerate fracture initiation. This explains why hot-rolled steel in seawater exhibited a 33.7% drop in elongation compared to 13.8% in cold-rolled steel, with a similar trend observed in NaCl. Cold-rolled retained 91.9% of its ductility, whereas hot-rolled dropped by 16.1%, highlighting the greater susceptibility of hot-rolled steel to localised chloride attack, likely due to its coarser grains and lower surface work-hardening. Acidic environments (HCl and H₂SO₄) produced the most dramatic losses in elongation, particularly for cold-rolled steel. In HCl, elongation dropped by 13.7% for cold-rolled specimens, while in H₂SO₄ a sharp 55.8% reduction occurred. This is attributed to severe uniform corrosion and hydrogen evolution, which cause thinning and promote hydrogen embrittlement—especially in metals with high dislocation density like cold-rolled steel. In contrast, hot-rolled steel showed better resistance, with only a 1.99% reduction in HCl and 17.4% in H₂SO₄. The lower internal stresses and coarser microstructure in hot-rolled steel slow hydrogen diffusion and delay crack initiation, enabling better ductility retention in acidic environments.

These trends are supported by fracture surface analysis, where specimens exposed to acids displayed brittle fracture features—sharp, angular surfaces and reduced necking—marking a transition in failure mode. This shift from ductile to brittle behaviour reflects a significant loss of energy absorption capacity, compromising structural integrity. Overall, the data emphasise that corrosive degradation not only reduces load capacity and mass but also critically alters failure mechanisms, especially in cold-rolled steel. These elongation trends are clearly visualised in Fig.  6 , illustrating how increasingly aggressive environments drive progressive embrittlement, particularly in cold-rolled steel. Each elongation value in Fig.  6  is the average of three independent tensile tests conducted under identical environmental conditions, with standard deviation values represented as error bars to reflect variability and ensure reproducibility. Fig. 6 Elongation at break of coupon specimens

sections.heading: Load carrying capacity of pipe specimens
paragraphs:
The variations in compressive load capacity of cold-rolled and hot-rolled mild steel pipe specimens after exposure to different corrosion environments (Table  4 , Fig.  7 ) reveal key relationships between environmental aggressiveness, material microstructure, and residual mechanical performance. In the nominal (unexposed) condition, the cold-rolled pipe exhibited a higher compressive strength (49 kN) than its hot-rolled counterpart (45.6 kN), attributable to its strain-hardened microstructure and higher dislocation density, which make cold-rolled steel inherently stronger in the absence of corrosion. However, this very feature becomes a liability in aggressive environments, as it increases susceptibility to localized corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement. Under air exposure, minimal corrosion occurred: the cold-rolled specimen retained its full load capacity, indicating that atmospheric oxygen and humidity did not compromise its mechanical integrity over the test duration, while the hot-rolled steel showed a minor 3.9% strength reduction, possibly due to surface oxidation or micro-pitting that slightly weakened the section. Tap water, though neutral in pH, induced mild electrochemical activity; the cold-rolled pipe lost 7.1% of its strength, compared with 4.8% for the hot-rolled specimen. The better performance of hot-rolled steel in this case may be linked to its coarser grain structure and lower internal stress levels, which enhance resistance to uniform corrosion and surface cracking. In seawater, a chloride-rich medium, the cold-rolled pipe showed minimal strength loss (0.41%), suggesting notable resistance to pitting-induced degradation, whereas the hot-rolled pipe experienced a 5.7% reduction, likely due to the localized attack of chloride ions on grain boundaries and inclusions—more prevalent in hot-rolled steel due to rolling scale and coarser microstructure. In NaCl solution, effects were more pronounced on the cold-rolled pipe, which suffered an 8.98% reduction compared to only 4.8% for the hot-rolled pipe, possibly due to accelerated localized corrosion from its high dislocation density. Acidic environments, particularly HCl and H₂SO₄, intensified corrosion due to low pH and active hydrogen ion participation in metal dissolution. HCl caused an 8.16% strength loss in cold-rolled pipes and 12.28% in hot-rolled ones, indicating that while both materials are vulnerable, hydrogen embrittlement and uniform thinning were more severe in hot-rolled steel, likely due to microstructural inclusions acting as corrosion initiation sites. The most severe deterioration occurred in H₂SO₄, where cold-rolled specimens lost 21.22% of their load capacity and hot-rolled ones lost 25%. The combination of sulfate ions and persistent acidity promoted aggressive uniform corrosion, leading to section loss and weakening of load paths, as corroborated by the visible deformation and thinning shown in Figs.  8 (a–g) and Figs.  9 (a–g).

Despite their higher initial strength, cold-rolled pipes are more vulnerable to highly aggressive chemical environments due to their microstructural characteristics, whereas hot-rolled pipes, although starting with slightly lower strength, retained mechanical performance better under moderate exposure conditions. Therefore, hot-rolled steel may be more suitable for environments with prolonged corrosion exposure where extreme aggressiveness, such as strong acid attack, is not anticipated.

sections.heading: Corrosion rate and thickness variation in coupon specimens
paragraphs:
Tables  5  and  6 , along with Figs.  10  and  11 , present a detailed assessment of corrosion behaviour in cold-rolled and hot-rolled steel coupon specimens over a 30-day immersion period in various environments. Corrosion rate values are based on three replicate specimens per condition. The observed standard deviation ranged from ± 0.01 to ± 0.12 mm/year, reflecting variability due to mass-loss fluctuations and differences in surface condition. Key parameters analysed include mass loss (converted to corrosion rate) and percentage reduction in thickness at 15 and 30 days. In an inert environment such as air, cold-rolled specimens showed negligible corrosion, with no weight loss until Day 15 and only a minor loss by Day 30, resulting in a corrosion rate of 0.109 mm/year. Hot-rolled specimens, while similarly stable, exhibited slightly higher rates—0.145 mm/year at 15 days and 0.217 mm/year at 30 days. Tap water caused only minor corrosion in both materials. Cold-rolled steel showed a corrosion rate of 0.145 mm/year at 15 days, which plateaued by Day 30. Hot-rolled specimens had a consistent rate of 0.217 mm/year, suggesting uniform corrosion behaviour over time. In seawater, cold-rolled steel remained largely unaffected until Day 15, followed by a slight increase in corrosion rate to 0.217 mm/year by Day 30. Hot-rolled steel showed gradual deterioration, with rates increasing from 0.072 mm/year to 0.181 mm/year, indicating continuous attack by chloride ions. In NaCl solution, cold-rolled steel experienced minimal degradation (maximum rate 0.072 mm/year). Hot-rolled steel, however, showed an anomalous weight increase at 15 days—possibly due to surface deposits—followed by a slight weight loss by Day 30, ending with a corrosion rate of 0.036 mm/year.

Acidic environments caused the most severe effects. Hydrochloric acid produced significant corrosion for both cold-rolled and hot-rolled specimens (4.563 mm/year each at 15 days), with decreasing rates at 30 days, suggesting possible surface passivation or saturation effects. Sulphuric acid exposure resulted in the highest corrosion rates: 10.212 mm/year (cold-rolled) and 9.488 mm/year (hot-rolled) at 15 days. By Day 30, rates reduced slightly but remained critically high—5.649 mm/year and 5.577 mm/year, respectively—indicating ongoing metal degradation and highlighting the aggressive nature of H₂SO₄. Thickness measurements further validate these corrosion trends. In neutral environments (air and tap water), cold-rolled specimens showed minimal change, with a maximum of 1.5–3% reduction by Day 30. Hot-rolled specimens, however, exhibited more pronounced thickness loss, particularly in tap water (11.5%) and seawater (6.5%). In NaCl solution, hot-rolled specimens again experienced a 6.5% thickness reduction by both Day 15 and Day 30, indicating rapid early corrosion with no further degradation thereafter. Cold-rolled samples showed better resistance, with only a 3.5% thickness loss. In acidic conditions, the reductions were dramatic. HCl caused 17% thickness loss in cold-rolled steel and 16% in hot-rolled steel by Day 30. H₂SO₄ was far more aggressive, reducing cold-rolled steel thickness by 30.5% and hot-rolled by 24%. sections.heading: Correlation of mechanical properties with exposure conditions
paragraphs:
The mechanical degradation of mild steel specimens exhibited a strong correlation with their chemical exposure environments, particularly in relation to pH levels and chloride ion concentrations. pH measurements were recorded in triplicate for each solution using a calibrated digital pH meter, with standard deviations ranging between ± 0.02 and ± 0.10, indicating minor variations due to corrosion product formation and solution interaction with steel surfaces. According to Table  7 , strong acids such as HCl and H₂SO₄ (initial pH 0) caused the most severe corrosion effects. This section provides a detailed analysis of the corrosion characteristics of cold-rolled and hot-rolled pipe specimens exposed to various environments over 30 days, covering pH variation, weight loss, thickness reduction, and corrosion rate to elucidate the underlying degradation mechanisms. In neutral environments such as tap water, cold-rolled pipes showed a steady pH increase from 7.9 to 8.92 over 30 days, indicating a mildly alkaline shift due to the formation of corrosion products (iron oxides/hydroxides). A similar, though less pronounced, trend was observed in hot-rolled samples. In seawater, pH changes were less predictable; cold-rolled samples showed a slight net increase to 7.96 at Day 15 before dropping to 7.2 by Day 30, while hot-rolled pipes followed a similar pattern, suggesting temporary passivation followed by continued corrosion and possible acidification. NaCl solutions displayed more erratic pH behavior. Cold-rolled pipes showed an initial alkalinity spike (6.86 to 7.8), followed by a sharp drop to 6.54, possibly due to localized corrosion or crevice attack. Hot-rolled pipes exhibited an opposite trend, starting acidic (5.65 at Day 15) and later returning near neutral, implying a dynamic electrochemical environment. In highly acidic media (HCl and H₂SO₄), the pH rose only slightly from 0 to ~ 2.5, indicating strong acid retention despite ongoing corrosion reactions. These trends are shown in Figs.  13  and  14 . Weight change data in Table  8  reflect the extent of corrosion. In air, cold-rolled steel showed negligible change (0.156% gain), likely due to surface oxidation. In tap water and seawater, weight loss remained modest (< 1%), confirming their relatively benign nature. In NaCl, both materials lost less than 0.6% mass, indicating mild corrosiveness compared to acids. HCl caused weight losses of 10.37% (cold-rolled) and 8.65% (hot-rolled), while H₂SO₄ was most destructive, with losses of 21.67% and 18.08%, respectively. Visual evidence is shown in Figs.  15  and  16 . Table  9  corroborates these findings, showing near-zero corrosion rates (< 0.01 mm/year) in air, slightly elevated rates (≤ 0.07 mm/year) in tap water and seawater, and low but notable rates (~ 0.04–0.05 mm/year) in NaCl. In contrast, acidic media produced high corrosion rates—HCl peaked at 1.70 mm/year (hot-rolled) and 1.67 mm/year (cold-rolled) within 15 days before decreasing, likely due to scale formation, while H₂SO₄ exhibited the most aggressive behavior, reaching 3.57 mm/year (hot-rolled) and 3.55 mm/year (cold-rolled). Thickness measurements in Table  10 , taken at multiple points along the pipe length, showed minimal variation (± 0.05 mm for cold-rolled, ± 0.08 mm for hot-rolled). In air and tap water, thickness reduction remained under 6%, confirming low corrosion activity, whereas in NaCl, losses reached 15.62% (cold-rolled) and 22.5% (hot-rolled), consistent with localized attack. Acidic environments proved to be the most damaging, particularly H₂SO₄, where cold-rolled pipes lost 38.12% of their thickness and hot-rolled pipes lost 36.5% over 30 days. These changes are shown in Figs.  17  and  18 , which illustrate the progression of material loss due to corrosion. Although the percentage weight loss of cold-rolled steel was higher in sulfuric acid (30.2%) compared to hot-rolled steel (24%), its residual load-bearing capacity was also higher (38.6 kN versus 34.2 kN). This apparent contradiction can be explained by the initial microstructural and mechanical properties of the material. Cold-rolled steel undergoes strain hardening during the rolling process, resulting in a higher dislocation density and greater initial strength. While corrosion caused significant mass loss and surface deterioration, the pre-existing strengthening effect allowed the cold-rolled steel to retain superior residual strength. In contrast, hot-rolled steel, with its typically more ductile and coarse-grained structure, has lower initial strength. Therefore, despite experiencing slightly less weight loss, it exhibited a greater relative reduction in load-bearing capacity. Moreover, surface damage from corrosion often exceeds its impact on the core mechanical durability, particularly over short exposure periods (30 days in this study). This explains why cold-rolled specimens maintained higher structural performance despite severe surface attack. A similar trend was observed under NaCl and HCl exposure, where cold-rolled specimens demonstrated better residual load capacity even when their surface corrosion parameters (weight loss and thickness loss) were comparable to, or slightly higher than, those of hot-rolled specimens. These findings highlight the need to assess not only surface corrosion metrics but also the core mechanical performance when selecting materials for structural applications in corrosive environments, especially where load-bearing capacity must be preserved under extreme conditions.

The pH variation of solutions containing cold-rolled and hot-rolled steel pipe specimens across different corrosion environments revealed distinct trends (Table  10 ). In neutral media such as tap water and NaCl, an overall increase in pH was observed due to the formation of alkaline corrosion products, with hot-rolled specimens exhibiting greater pH shifts, indicating higher initial corrosion activity. In seawater, cold-rolled steel showed relatively stable pH levels, whereas hot-rolled steel displayed slight acidification over time, suggesting more active corrosion. In highly acidic environments (HCl and H₂SO₄), both steel types caused an increase in pH due to hydrogen ion consumption, with cold-rolled specimens generally showing slightly greater neutralisation, indicating more aggressive corrosion (Table  11 ).

The pH variation trends of cold-rolled and hot-rolled pipe specimens across different corrosion environments are shown in Figs.  19  and  20 . In both cases, exposure to neutral solutions such as tap water and seawater resulted in an increase in pH during the first 15 days, followed by a slight decline by day 30. This behaviour suggests the initial formation of alkaline corrosion products, with possible stabilisation or surface passivation over time. In acidic environments (HCl and H₂SO₄), the pH increased gradually, indicating active corrosion and the neutralisation of hydrogen ions. Notably, cold-rolled specimens (Fig.  19 ) exhibited slightly higher pH levels than hot-rolled specimens (Fig.  20 ), implying more pronounced corrosion-induced alkalinity. In NaCl solution, hot-rolled specimens showed an initial pH drop followed by recovery, reflecting early aggressive corrosion and subsequent stabilisation, whereas cold-rolled pipes displayed a relatively stable pH rise. Overall, hot-rolled steel tended to exhibit greater fluctuations in pH, indicating a potentially more reactive surface and higher corrosion activity, particularly in chloride-rich environments. In this study, the smooth trend lines shown in all scatter plots are intended solely to aid visual interpretation of corrosion progression between the measured intervals (15 and 30 days). Given the limited number of data points, these lines are not intended for predictive modelling or extrapolation. Actual measurement points are clearly marked to ensure accurate representation of the data. Future studies will incorporate more frequent early-stage measurements (e.g., 1, 3, and 7 days) to capture initial corrosion kinetics more precisely.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study confirms that cold-rolled mild steel experiences higher corrosion rates and greater mechanical deterioration than hot-rolled steel in aggressive acidic environments (H₂SO₄ and HCl), due to its finer microstructure and higher dislocation density. Sulfuric acid exposure caused extreme reductions in elongation and thickness, highlighting a critical vulnerability that has not been widely quantified before. Both hot-rolled and cold-rolled mild steel exhibited severe corrosion in H₂SO₄ and HCl solutions, with peak corrosion rates occurring at 15 days followed by a decline by day 30. In contrast, minimal corrosion was observed in air, tap water, and NaCl environments, with corrosion rates remaining below 0.2 mm/year. The thickness ratio (t₃₀/t₀) fell below 0.75 in acidic media, confirming significant material loss, whereas in milder environments it remained above 0.935. Hot-rolled samples generally experienced greater thickness reduction than cold-rolled samples. Cold-rolled coupons showed up to a 55.76% reduction in elongation, most notably in H₂SO₄, while hot-rolled samples retained more elongation, especially in HCl. Mechanical strength declined significantly in acidic environments: cold-rolled samples lost up to 39.25% strength (H₂SO₄), and hot-rolled samples up to 37%. In air and neutral solutions, strength loss was minimal. Acidic exposures caused pH increases over time due to neutralization reactions, whereas other environments showed minimal pH changes, indicating limited chemical interaction.

Pipe specimens mirrored coupon results, with significant weight loss (up to 21.66% in H₂SO₄) and more than 30% loss in load capacity in acidic conditions.While hot-rolled specimens exhibited better short-term corrosion resistance, this behavior is likely influenced by the presence of mill scale—a thin iron oxide layer formed during hot rolling—which temporarily reduces the permeability of corrosive agents and delays active corrosion. However, once this protective layer deteriorates under prolonged or aggressive exposure, the underlying steel—characterized by microstructural features such as coarse grain boundaries, inclusions, and residual stress—may corrode more rapidly than cold-rolled steel. This progressive degradation was not fully captured within the 30-day immersion period used in this study. The aggressive environments used in the study were intended for accelerated comparison and do not simulate actual field conditions. Therefore, the findings should not be directly extrapolated to real-world service life predictions without further validation through long-term exposure studies.

Overall, cold-rolled samples showed higher corrosion rates and mechanical degradation under aggressive conditions, while hot-rolled specimens maintained relatively better short-term structural integrity. The study uniquely correlates mechanical performance under simultaneous corrosive and mechanical stresses, providing practical insights for material selection in acid-exposed environments. However, limitations such as the short test duration, absence of microstructural and surface roughness analysis, and the lack of in-situ corrosion tracking may influence the interpretation of long-term performance. Future work should focus on understanding the kinetics of F1M scale breakdown and its impact on corrosion progression through extended-duration studies. Employing advanced techniques such as in-situ electrochemical monitoring, surface and microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, EBSD, and XRD), and longer-term field simulations will be essential. Additionally, evaluating green corrosion inhibitors may contribute to the development of more sustainable protection strategies for structural steel in aggressive environments.
